# Summary {#part-orchestration-summary .unnumbered}

Part VI widened the unit of work from a completion to a task. The model now has to act through loops, tools, memory, retrieval, context assembly, and sometimes other agents. The harness, the runtime around the model, becomes part of the system's behavior. It controls which state is visible and which evidence is admitted, limits the tools a step is allowed to call, and determines what happens after a step fails.

The risk grows with that surrounding machinery. An ordinary model error can now turn into a side effect in an external system. Memory serves as evidence and as liability at once, and when it outlives the task and becomes the product's memory of its user, it also becomes a switching cost and an attack surface. Retrieval can bring untrusted text into the prompt, where the model may follow it as instructions; an agent operating a screen reads whatever an attacker can render on it; and agents in a multi-agent debate can reproduce a shared mistake without exposing it. For each of these risks, the part asked which loop owns the next decision and what can interrupt it.

The part treated orchestration as the engineering of decision loops around a model, in which state, authority, retrieval, interruption, and recovery matter as much as the model call. The open question is which agent patterns remain reliable under production load, adversarial input, tenant boundaries, and changing tool permissions, and answering it requires instruments that measure a whole agent run. Part VII supplies that instrument layer: when a system acts through a loop, evaluation has to measure the evidence, side effects, and changed state the run leaves behind, as well as the answer.
